Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents:
Try something different:

Any computer can be a server. An old laptop, a Raspberry Pi, ex gaming PCs, but there are many computers you'll see on places like Facebook Marketplace that don't look like they'd be good server material, even though on the inside they're exactly what you're looking for.

✕ Remove Ads

These “boring” old business PCs are secretly perfect for home servers

Business in the front, homelab in the back

The typical Dell, HP, or Lenovo office PC is built to be unremarkable. Which is a good thing! These are workhorses meant to work day in and day out without spending too much time in the IT department. They are built to a price, sure, but easy maintenance and reliability are a design goal.

They also tend to have decent CPUs. While RAM counts might be a little low for desktop use, and there's unlikely to be lots of storage or GPU power, they almost always have a decent multicore CPU designed to handle productivity apps.

These PCs are so cheap on the used market, because they've gone through a full depreciation cycle, not because they were cheaply made or poor quality.

How to actually find the good stuff on Facebook Marketplace

Hiding in (very) plain sight

That said, there's a lot of variation on the inside, even when all of these corporate office boxes look the same. The first step is to use the right keyword to filter all but the best stuff. Here are some good ones to try:

✕ Remove Ads
  • OptiPlex
  • ProDesk / EliteDesk
  • ThinkCentre

You might also have some luck searching for "Office PC" or "i5 desktop" in the hope that someone who knows nothing about computers might sell one of these corporate office PCs for much less than it's actually worth. What's important is that you familiarize yourself with the upmarket branding names for the nicer class of mass-produced office PC. The one your manager gets to use, not the cashiers.

How to tell if a cheap PC is actually worth buying

Ignoring the fool's gold

Once you're looking at the right brand and tier of used PC, it's time to get into the details. On the performance side of things, it really only matters what you intend to do with the server. Compare the CPU in the system you're looking at against the recommended requirements and decide whether it will do the job or not. You might expect this to be the big set of decisions, but it's really just a matter of matching the CPU to the job, and ensuring you can install as much RAM as you'll need.

The best general guidance I can give is to aim for a PC with at least a 6th-generation Intel CPU or equivalent. If you're going to run Windows 11 on this system, you need to use the Windows 11 minimum requirements as a guide. 8GB of RAM is the bare minimum, but if you can upgrade later it's not that important. If you're building a Plex or Jellyfin server, Intel Quick Sync or another compatible acceleration technology is crucial if you need to do real-time transcoding.

Now, the truly important issue here is the form factor. For example, I've often advocated for mini PCs to be used as home servers, but that will limit you in significant ways. Any additional hard drives will have to be external, and you can't add expansion cards.

✕ Remove Ads

However, if it meets your needs, it can be a great solution. For example, I bought this dual-core Lenovo mini PC for about $30 to serve as a Plex server. It does this job perfectly, and my content is stored on external drives connected with a hub. Spending more on a bigger or better computer would be a waste of money because it does the job already.

✕ Remove Ads

You can, of course, choose to buy a full traditional PC tower, and there's nothing wrong with that. You can stuff it with drives and expansion cards and make any upgrades or modifications you want. As long as the price is right, this is the most flexible option. However, it's not space or power efficient.

Which is why I think the most interesting option for home server use is an SFF (Small Form Factor) PC.

✕ Remove Ads

These have smaller power supplies and are built to take up little space and not make noise. Yet, you might still get a few internal drive bays and the option to add one or two small expansion cards. The CPU might be swappable too. SFF cases are also easier to open and work inside compared to mini PCs.

What you need to turn it into a home server

Once you have your PC, and want to turn it into a server, you'll need the following:

✕ Remove Ads
  • An operating system such as Windows, or a flavor of Linux. If you like, you can use server-specific versions, but it's not strictly necessary. Consider specialist OSes like TrueNAS if you're building a very specialized server.
  • You'll need a flash drive large enough to accommodate the OS installation files and an app like Rufus to prep the flash drive with those files so you can boot from it.
  • Additional storage is probably necessary, depending on the job. Recertified enterprise hard drives are often a good choice.
  • In some cases, you might need a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. However, most people only use these for the initial setup, and then use remote access software to operate the server thereafter.

The last piece of the puzzle is an Ethernet connection, which most of these PCs should already have. However, you might have to add one, or at least a faster one using USB or an expansion slot. While you can connect your server to your home network with Wi-Fi, it's not a recipe for stable performance. Good luck and have fun!
